## Introduction

The N170 is an event-related potential (ERP) component that helps explain how the brain responds to faces. It is a negative response, which is plotted upwards, and peaks at around 170 milliseconds (ms) after a stimulus is presented (@kappenman2021). The response is stimulus-locked, meaning it is measured relative to stimulus onset, and is usually examined within a -200–800 ms epoch window (@kappenman2021). The N170 is commonly measured at PO8, which is located over areas involved in visual processing and memory. Compared with non-face objects, faces are expected to produce a larger N170 response because they are meaningful visual stimuli that require specialised processing (@eimer2011). Processing of faces is thought to involve the inferior temporal cortex, especially the fusiform gyrus, which plays a role in recognising faces and remembering people we are familiar with (@eimer2011).

### History of the N170
Bentin et al. first identified the N170 response in a study designed to define a facial recognition ERP (@bentin1996). The stimuli included non-target objects (e.g., butterflies), distorted objects (e.g., noses), inverted faces, and target objects (e.g., famous faces and random faces). The study showed a negative 172ms response in the posterior temporal scalp when participants viewed a target object, with the N170 response being strongest in the right hemisphere of the brain. The researchers also found that isolated eyes elicited a larger N170 than whole faces, suggesting that the component may be particularly sensitive to eye information. Bentin et al. proposed that the N170 may reflect a neural mechanism involved in detecting human faces and suggested it may relate to the face-selective N200 response recorded from the parietooccipital region (@bentin1996). 

### Controversies
The N170 is controversial due to the neurological mechanisms underlying how the fusiform gyrus recognises faces. For instance, some studies of the N170 component have found the face inversion effect, in which more energy is put into encoding distorted and inverted faces in comparison to other items and regular faces (@kanwisher1998). Researchers also debate whether the difficulty in processing inverted faces stems from spatial reconstruction (@rossion2008) or post-processing encoding errors (@itier2002). The inverse face effect underscores how the fusiform gyrus is sensitive to facial features. A meta-analysis (@carretie2013) found that in contrast to earlier studies which found the N170 was insensitive to facial expression, the N170 is influenced by the expression of emotions. Specifically, anger, happiness and fear elicited the largest N170 response in comparison to neutral faces (@carretie2013).

Another important area of N170 research is how face familiarity affects the response. Caheral found that familiar faces, including the participant’s own face and famous faces, produced larger N170 amplitudes than unfamiliar faces (@caheral2002). The study suggests that familiarity is closely associated with a strong N170 response. The N170 is also affected by repetition. When the same face is shown twice in quick succession, the N170 response is reduced (@jemel2005). Interestingly, different faces presented in succession produced similar amplitudes per face. In addition, Campatelli found that people or individuals living with autism spectrum disorders have underestimated facial recognition processing abilities and produce a similar N170 responses (@campatelli2013). Overall, these studies show that the N170 is affected not only by whether a stimulus is a face, but also by factors such as familiarity, repetition, and individual differences in face processing. The present study will use data from @kappenman2021 and will follow most of the same preprocessing procedures, except for the filtering steps.

## Methods

The present study will use data from @kappenman2021 and the ERP CORE resource under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0). 

### Participants

Data were collected from 40 healthy neurotypical, native English-speaking participants from the University of California, Davis Community. Participants were excluded if the trials exceeded 25% artifacts or achieved less than 75% accuracy on the tasks. The distribution included 25 female and 15 male participants (mean age = 21.5, SD = 2.87; range 18–30; 38 right-handed. After applying the preprocessing criteria, three participants were excluded because more than 25% of their trials were rejected due to artifacts, leaving fewer than 50% usable face trials. The final sample included 13 males and 24 females (mean age = 21.5, SD = 7.78; range 18-30, 35; right-handed).

```{python}
exclude = ["001", "005", "016"]
```


### Procedure
Participants completed face perception tasks in which a stimulus, such as a target (face) or a non-target (scrambled face, car, or scrambled car), was presented at the centre of the screen at intervals of 1600-1800ms. Participants were then asked to identify the target type (face or car) and its quality (scrambled or non-scrambled).EEG recording. 


### EEG recording

The system used to record the electroencephalography (EEG) was a Biosemi ActiveTwo recording system. The cap had 30 electrodes systemised in the international 10/20 (FP1, F3, F7, FC3, C3, C5, P3, P7, P9, PO7, PO3, O1, Oz, Pz, CPz, FP2, Fz, F4, F8, FC4, FCz, Cz, C4, C6, P4, P8, P10, PO8, PO4, O2). All signals passed through a low-pass with a 0.1 cut-off and a high-pass filter with a 30 Hz cut-off. Vertical electrooculogram (VEOG) was recorded from below the right eye, while the horizontal electrooculogram (HEOG) was recorded on the lateral side of the eye. Referencing for the N170 was done via averaging all 30 electrodes, with the bipolar HEOG being computed through left HEOG minus right HEOG, while bipolar VEOG was computed through lower VEOG minus FP2 (@kappenman2021). 

### Analysis parameters

Analysis and processing were conducted in MATLAB using the EEGLAB and ERPLAB toolboxes. To increase processing speed, EEG and Electrooculography (EOG) were downsampled to 256Hz. EEG signals were recorded from 30 sites and then averaged. Large voltage artifacts in the trials that survived the data segmentation process were then excluded. The HEOG also allowed the removal of trials with excessive eye movements (e.g., blinks and horizontal movements). Horizontal and vertical eye movements may also affect event-locked stimulus responses, so we also carefully analysed and excluded these using the original data. Incorrect responses and excessively fast/slow trials were also excluded, leaving those with an acceptable response time of 200ms-1000ms. 

#### Preprocessing parameters

```{python}

FILTER_SETTINGS = {
    "low_cutoff": 0.1,
    "high_cutoff": 30.0
}


REFERENCE = None

```

#### Epoching parameters

```{python}
TMIN = -0.2 
TMAX = 0.8 

BASELINE = (-0.2,0) 


CONDITIONS = ["stimulus/face", "stimulus/car", "stimulus/scrambled_face", "stimulus/scrambled_car"]

REJECT = {
    "eeg": 150e-6,
    "eog": 250e-6
}

```

## Data analysis

### Preprocessing
 
```{python}
#| eval: false 
#| output: false 

for raw_file in RAW_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz"):

    
    subj_ID = raw_file.stem.split("_")[0]

    
    raw = SimpleRaw(raw_file)

    
    
    processed = preprocess(raw, 
                            reref_params = REFERENCE, 
                            filter_low_cutoff = FILTER_SETTINGS["low_cutoff"], 
                            filter_high_cutoff = FILTER_SETTINGS["high_cutoff"])
    
    processed.save(PROCESSED_PATH / f"{subj_ID}_raw.fif.gz", overwrite = True)


```

### Epoching and averaging

```{python}
#| output: false


ss_avs = {}

for cond in CONDITIONS:
    ss_avs[cond] = []

for processed_file in PROCESSED_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz"):
    subj_ID = processed_file.stem.split("_") [0]
    if subj_ID in exclude:
        continue
    
    processed = SimpleRaw(processed_file)

    
    events, event_id = processed.get_events()

    
    epochs = SimpleEpoch(processed, events, event_id, tmin = TMIN, tmax = TMAX, baseline = BASELINE, reject = REJECT)

    
    for cond in CONDITIONS:
        av = epochs[cond].average()
        ss_avs[cond].append(av)

```

### Grand average

```{python}
#| output: false


grand_avs = {}

for cond in CONDITIONS:
    grand = grand_average(ss_avs[cond])
    grand_avs[cond] = grand
```

## Results

### Grand average: N170


```{python}
selected_electrode = "PO8"
plot_title = "Grand average for N170 responces"
analysis_window_start = 1.1
analysis_window_end = 1.5

plot_evokeds(grand_avs, picks = selected_electrode, invert_y = True, title = plot_title, vlines = [analysis_window_start, analysis_window_end])


```

## Discussion and reflection

The results suggest that intact faces produced the largest N170 response, while intact cars, scrambled faces, and scrambled cars produced smaller responses. The results broadly align with @kappenman2021, which found that faces produced a larger and earlier N170 response than cars. However, @kappenman2021 mainly focused on the comparison between intact faces and cars in their figures, even though scrambled face and car stimuli were also used in the experiment. The scrambled stimuli were expected to produce smaller N170 responses because they retained some visual features but lacked the meaningful configuration of an intact face or car. As @kappenman2021 used neutral faces, future research could test whether emotional facial expressions affect the N170 response. Future studies could also vary the degree of scrambling, or scramble only specific facial regions, to further determine which facial features are most important for producing the N170 response.

Reflecting on the coding process has made me realise the importance of avoiding repetition and following the don’t repeat yourself (DRY) principle. At first, I copied and pasted lines of code because rewriting them seemed quicker, but copying and pasting often caused errors when I ran the cells in order. I also learned that a small mistake, such as not updating the referencing code, can affect the whole analysis and the results reported.In the future, I will aim to rewrite necessary code and attempt to follow the DRY principle by thoroughly examining cells one at a time rather than running the whole program. I will also need to practice with dummy sets of data to further improve my skills in coding, in turn improving my eye for noticing mistakes in codes. Overall, this process has taught me that coding is not only about getting the analysis to run, but also about making it clear, accurate, and easy to reproduce.
